z-m-07-09.title: How many red-bean buns bakery suppose bake next Monday?
z-m-07-09.topic: Predicting future from sales records (handling outlier)
z-m-07-09.goal: Learn how outlier handling depend on its reason when predicting from records; update guess and confidence with new information, write note.
z-m-07-09.material: Neighborhood bakery bake red-bean buns each morning for that day's sale. Too many leave leftovers; too few run out. Owner use last-week sales to decide next Monday amount. Shop open Monday to Friday last week.
z-m-07-09.thinking.1: Handling outlier by checking its reason
z-m-07-09.thinking.2: Keeping or revising judgment with new info
z-m-07-09.thinking.3: Noting situations where guess might change
z-m-07-09.prereq.0: Reading table numbers and separating close values from outliers (Grade 3)
z-m-07-09.s.s1.prompt: Let's estimate next Monday amount as sales records come out bit by bit. Each stage, choose best guess.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write known daily sales in order; mark values close together and those far away.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.hint.1: If one number far away, think how to check if something else happen that day.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: About how many buns good to bake next Monday?
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.0.after: Three days similar, 12 to 14, so about 13 or with extra about 14 reasonable. Only 3 days known, so wanting more data fair, but current records still give rough scale.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: That's much more than highest sale among three days. See whether records give reason for such a big increase.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This judgment choose middle since three-day sales close, 12 to 14.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This judgment allow little extra because shortage worse than leftovers.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.0.o.d: We only see 3 days, can't decide
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Careful attitude, but closeness among three days still clue.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.1.info: Thursday sold 31. Owner no know why.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: How your guess for next Monday change?
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.1.after: Without knowing reason for 31, both keeping about 13 while investigating and preparing more generously, 17 to 18, make sense. Both avoid trusting or deleting 31 without basis.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Raise amount near 31 because latest record
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Is recentness reason to trust 31? How different from other three days?
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: No evidence record wrong. Better investigate high sales reason than erase without proof.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Keep first guess but find why Thursday high
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This judgment neither trust nor erase far-off value immediately; it investigates cause.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Add all four days, divide by 4, bake about 17 to 18
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Outlier still record so include am, but e raise average. We no know whether next Monday resemble Thursday.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.2.info: Friday sold 13. We learn Thursday had one-time fair nearby. No event next Monday.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now, about how many bake next Monday?
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.2.after: Thursday high because one-time event; no event Monday, so other four days (12,14,13,13) better guide. About 13 or with room about 15 reasonable. Even student who kept first guess can be more confident after learning reason. Sales for the other 4 days were 12, 14, 13, 13.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.2.r.a: They say no event next Monday. Think if reason for 31 happen again.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.2.r.b: How did you reflect in calculation that Thursday was event day, not ordinary?
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Leave out event Thursday; other days close 12 to 14. This picks their middle.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This gives extra room based on about 13.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.reflect: Including 31 or leaving out Thursday changes guess a lot. Explain why you treated same value differently before/after learning reason. Could one-time event happen again?
z-m-07-09.s.s2.prompt: Write note to owner: next Monday amount, why, and one situation that could change it.
z-m-07-09.s.s2.hint.0: Read close-to-Monday days again and find most similar one.
z-m-07-09.s.s2.hint.1: Think one situation that could change amount (event, weather).
z-m-07-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: You check chosen amount close to record values?
z-m-07-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You explain how you handle Thursday 31 and why?
z-m-07-09.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Situation you name really could change bun count?
z-m-07-09.s.s2.model.0: I suggest about 13. Mon, Tue, Wed and Fri sold 12 to 14; Thursday 31 was fair event. If event nearby Monday too, bake more.
z-m-07-09.s.s2.model.1: I'll bake about 15. Usually about 13 sell, so add 2 extra. Leave out Thursday 31 because one-time event. If rain, fewer might sell.
z-m-07-09.s.s2.modelNote.1: This note leaves some extra stock.

z-m-07-01.title: Is product of two-digit number times one-digit number always three digits?
z-m-07-01.topic: Deciding digit count of (two-digit number)×(one-digit number)
z-m-07-01.goal: Learn few correct examples no prove 'always'; make own examples where product is two digits, and say when it becomes three digits.
z-m-07-01.material:
Doyun calculate multiplication and talk:
'37×4=148, 52×6=312, 78×9=702. Product of two-digit number and one-digit number always get three digits!'
(Here, two-digit number na 10 to 99, and one-digit na 2 to 9. 37×4 you read 'thirty-seven times four.')
z-m-07-01.thinking.0: Checking if many correct examples guarantee 'always'
z-m-07-01.thinking.2: Stating criterion that separates when true and false
z-m-07-01.prereq.0: Reading two-digit by one-digit multiplication expressions (Grade 3)
z-m-07-01.s.s1.prompt: Wetin you think about Doyun? Judge within ranges: two-digit numbers 10 to 99, one-digit 2 to 9.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.hint.0: Put Doyun tested numbers 37, 52, 78 and multipliers 4, 6, 9 side by side; find cases he never test.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.hint.1: Multiply two smallest values and two biggest, estimate product range.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.o.a: You multiply by one-digit, so product always two-digit
z-m-07-01.s.s1.r.a: A two-digit number as one factor no mean product two-digit. Check digits in 78×9 example Doyun gave.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.o.b: If one-digit factor 9, product always three-digit
z-m-07-01.s.s1.r.b: Even times 9 fit give two-digit. Look at 10×9.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.o.c: All three examples correct, so Doyun right
z-m-07-01.s.s1.r.c: Correct examples no same as 'always' correct. Check whether untested cases dey.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.o.d: Sometimes product get three digits, sometimes two
z-m-07-01.s.s1.r.d: Product digit count fit depend on factor sizes. Make examples and check.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.explain: Smallest product in range na 10×2=20; largest 99×9=891. So product fit be two or three digits, no four.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.prompt: Make two examples with different products to show Doyun wrong. Choose two-digit a (10-99) and one-digit b (2-9) so product no get three digits.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.hint.0: Start with small numbers, multiply, and check product digit count.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.hint.1: Choose one a, then change b to 2, 3, 4, ... and find when product first get three digits.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Make a natural number from 10 to 99.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Make b natural number from 2 to 9.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.ok.c3: Product less than 100, so no be three digits. Doyun claim don fail.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.fail.c3: Product get three digits or more. Make a or b smaller.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.explain: For example, 12×3=36, 20×4=80, 45×2=90 all get two digits. 50×2=100 na start of three-digit numbers, so no be counterexample. One counterexample enough to break 'always.'
z-m-07-01.s.s3.prompt: Wetin you wan tell Doyun? Use examples to explain why wrong and when product become three digits.
z-m-07-01.s.s3.hint.0: You fit use expressions from examples you just made.
z-m-07-01.s.s3.hint.1: Think what number separate two-digit and three-digit numbers.
z-m-07-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: For your example, did you calculate again to check product really get two digits?
z-m-07-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You state one example enough to break 'always'?
z-m-07-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You state with numbers when it becomes three digits, like 99×9, or criterion 100 or more?
z-m-07-01.s.s3.model.0: Doyun no always correct. Some cases two-digit, like 12×3=36. If factors big and product reach 100 or more, e get three digits.
z-m-07-01.s.s3.model.1: No. 20×4=80 has two digits. Bigger factors give bigger product, so fit become three digits like 99×9=891.
z-m-07-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: Answer saying 'bigger numbers' instead of criterion '100 or more' okay too.
z-m-07-01.s.s3.model.2: Two-digit product fit happen, like 12×3=36, so Doyun wrong. Product must reach 100 to be three digits.

z-m-07-03.title: I divide the number for one card by 6 and quotient na 7. Wetin be the number for card?
z-m-07-03.topic: Find range of dividend from quotient and remainder for division with remainder
z-m-07-03.goal: Know say quotient alone no fix dividend as one number, point out the missing information (remainder), then find different numbers wey meet the conditions and the biggest number.
z-m-07-03.material: Soyul cover one number card with her hand and talk, 'The number for this card na natural number. I divide am by 6 and quotient na 7.' Soyul never talk whether remainder dey or not.
z-m-07-03.thinking.1: Make different numbers wey meet the conditions
z-m-07-03.thinking.2: Explain the range wey remainder fit be
z-m-07-03.prereq.0: Know wetin quotient and remainder mean for division with remainder (Grade 3 level)
z-m-07-03.s.s1.prompt: Words from Soyul alone fit fix the number for card to just one? Wetin else you need know to fix am to one?
z-m-07-03.s.s1.hint.0: First write the smallest number wey quotient na 7. Add 1, 2, 3, ... to am and check whether quotient still be 7.
z-m-07-03.s.s1.hint.1: Write all the possible numbers and find one more piece of information wey go leave only one.
z-m-07-03.s.s1.o.a: You need know more about how big the remainder be
z-m-07-03.s.s1.r.a: Even if quotient same, if remainder different, dividend different. If you know remainder, you fit choose just one of the possible numbers.
z-m-07-03.s.s1.o.b: You need know more whether e odd or even
z-m-07-03.s.s1.r.b: If you know odd or even, the possible numbers go reduce, but no be only one. Count how many even candidates and odd candidates you fit make.
z-m-07-03.s.s1.o.c: You need know more whether the divisor 6 correct
z-m-07-03.s.s1.r.c: Soyul don already tell us say divisor na 6. Wetin never fix na another part.
z-m-07-03.s.s1.r.d: 42 na one of the possible numbers, but if remainder dey, e no be 42. Soyul no talk say e divide exact.
z-m-07-03.s.s1.explain: Wen quotient na 7, the number for card na one of 42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47 (remainder na 0 to 5). If you know remainder, you fit fix am to one. If you only know odd or even, 3 numbers remain each.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.prompt: Make we say the number for card no divide exact by 6. Write 3 different numbers for card wey get quotient 7 and remainder.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether remainder dey after you subtract 6 from the number on card 7 times.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.hint.1: Divide each number from 42 to 48 by 6 one after another, and check whether quotient na 7 and remainder no be 0.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The number for card na natural number.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Make the number for card natural number wey be 1 or more.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Quotient after dividing by 6 no be 7. Count how many times you fit remove 6.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.fail.c3: E divide exact by 6. Change am to number wey remainder no be 0.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.explain: Numbers wey get quotient 7 and remainder na 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, five numbers. Dem be 42 plus remainders 1 to 5.
z-m-07-03.s.s3.prompt: Wetin be the biggest number wey the number on card fit be? Explain why na that one be biggest by connecting am with remainder.
z-m-07-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write possible remainder numbers starting from 0 one by one and see where you must stop.
z-m-07-03.s.s3.hint.1: Compare am with the smallest number wey quotient na 8.
z-m-07-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You check say dividing the number you write by 6 really give quotient 7?
z-m-07-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You talk why remainder no fit be 6 or more?
z-m-07-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You write the connection say wen remainder biggest, dividend too biggest?
z-m-07-03.s.s3.model.0: Na 47. Remainder must be less than divisor 6, so biggest remainder na 5. 42 plus 5 na 47.
z-m-07-03.s.s3.model.1: Na 47. Wen dem divide by 6, remainder fit only be 0 to 5, so wen remainder na 5, 42+5=47 na the biggest.
z-m-07-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: Na explanation wey start with 6×7=42 and add the remainder.

z-m-07-07.title: When 75-minute swim class on notice go finish?
z-m-07-07.topic: Calculating clock time and duration (minutes), reading notice
z-m-07-07.goal: Check whether notice time details fix one ending time; identify missing info (whether break included) and rewrite so guardians no misunderstand.
z-m-07-07.material:
Swim-class notice say:
'Class starts 3:40 p.m. Class last 75 minutes, with a 10-minute break halfway.'
Guardians meeting start 5:00 p.m. Class must end at 5:00 or before for guardians attend. (3:40 read 'three forty.')
z-m-07-07.thinking.1: Finding several times wey fit conditions
z-m-07-07.prereq.0: Reading time of day and duration (hours/minutes), 1 hour = 60 minutes (Grade 3)
z-m-07-07.s.s1.prompt: Can notice alone fix one ending time? What else needed?
z-m-07-07.s.s1.hint.1: Read sentences one by one: how '75 minutes' and '10-minute break' relate? Any place different readers fit read differently?
z-m-07-07.s.s1.o.a: Need know more about class starting time
z-m-07-07.s.s1.r.a: Start time (3:40 p.m.) already on notice. Look what still no fixed.
z-m-07-07.s.s1.o.b: Need know travel time from pool to home
z-m-07-07.s.s1.r.b: Travel time home no concern class finish time. Lesson length decides end.
z-m-07-07.s.s1.o.c: Need know whether break included in 75 minutes
z-m-07-07.s.s1.r.c: End time differ by 10 minutes depending if break included. Separate both cases and compare.
z-m-07-07.s.s1.o.d: E fit fix. All needed numbers dey
z-m-07-07.s.s1.r.d: Even if all numbers dey, sentence no fix how dem connect. Think where break go.
z-m-07-07.s.s1.explain: If break inside 75 min, end 4:55 p.m.; otherwise 10 minutes later, 5:05. Notice no say which. Difference matter for ending by 5:00.
z-m-07-07.s.s2.prompt: If count 75-minute class and 10-minute break separately, total class period 85 minutes. For class end 5:00 or earlier, what minute after 3 o'clock must it start? Write 3 starting times in 5-minute steps. (For 3:s, write s; s 0 to 59.)
z-m-07-07.s.s2.hint.0: Change 85 minutes to hours and minutes.
z-m-07-07.s.s2.hint.1: Choose start time, find time 85 minutes later, and see whether before 5:00 sharp.
z-m-07-07.s.s2.var.s: Start time: 3 o'clock and p minutes, p.m.
z-m-07-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Make s a natural number from 0 to 59.
z-m-07-07.s.s2.explain: 85 minutes na 1 hour 25 min. 1h25 before 5:00 na 3:35. So if class start 3:35 or earlier, e end by 5. In 5-minute steps, 3:00, 3:05, ... to 3:35 all work. 5:00 sharp.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite notice so nobody misunderstand. Choose whether break inside 75 minutes. For guardians to get one end time, say class start 3:40 p.m., write clear end time and where break fit.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.hint.0: Find 75 minutes after 3:40, then decide whether add 10-minute break.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.hint.1: Rewrite in one sentence the part of first notice wey readers fit understand two ways.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: End time in your notice match explanation you choose (break included or no)?
z-m-07-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Part readers fit read two ways before now only has one meaning?
z-m-07-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You write both start and end clearly with hours/minutes?
z-m-07-07.s.s3.model.0: Class start 3:40 p.m. and ends 5:05. Count 75-minute class and 10-minute break separately: total 85 minutes.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.modelNote.0: This notice for case where break count separately.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.model.1: Starts 3:40 and ends 5:05. 10-minute break no dey inside 75-minute class.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.model.2: Class starts 3:40 and ends 4:55. 10-minute break dey inside 75 min.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.modelNote.2: This notice for case where break included within 75 minutes.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.model.3: Class starts 3:40 and ends 4:55. 10-minute break included in 75-minute class.

z-m-07-08.title: Can we know combined result without each class vote count?
z-m-07-08.topic: Reading two vote results together (difference information)
z-m-07-08.goal: Learn say combining votes need 'how many more', not each class total. Check/explain by making examples with different vote numbers.
z-m-07-08.material:
Grade 3 Class 1 and Class 2 vote for field-trip place: zoo or museum, each cast one vote.
Class 1: zoo get 3 votes more than museum.
Class 2: museum get 2 more than zoo.
We no know total votes or individual counts for either class. School combine both votes and choose majority.
z-m-07-08.thinking.1: Making several examples that fit conditions
z-m-07-08.prereq.0: Reading vote counts in table and comparing (Grade 3)
z-m-07-08.prereq.1: Experience combining results of two classes
z-m-07-08.s.s1.prompt: If combine votes, which place get how many more? Can we tell?
z-m-07-08.s.s1.hint.0: Choose one vote set fitting Class 1 and one for Class 2, combine totals.
z-m-07-08.s.s1.hint.1: Choose different vote numbers again and see if combined difference change.
z-m-07-08.s.s1.r.a: This judgment consider combined difference when zoo ahead in one class and museum in other. Check with example.
z-m-07-08.s.s1.o.b: We can't tell; need each class vote count
z-m-07-08.s.s1.r.b: Even without class totals, knowing 'how many more' lets you find combined difference. Choose example counts and add.
z-m-07-08.s.s1.r.c: Think where 3 and 5 come from. Museum ahead in Class 2. How reflect that in combined result?
z-m-07-08.s.s1.r.d: Combined vote total decide, no number of classes won. Lead by 3 and lead by 2 are different sizes.
z-m-07-08.s.s1.explain: Example: Class 1 14 to 11, Class 2 9 to 11. Combined zoo 23, museum 22, zoo ahead 1. Another: Class 1 5 to 2, Class 2 3 to 5; zoo 8, museum 7, again 1 ahead. Even if class totals differ, if only know leads, combined zoo margin 1 (3 minus 2).
z-m-07-08.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 examples with different voter counts where Class 1 zoo leads by 3, Class 2 museum by 2. Class 1 z1 zoo, b1 museum; Class 2 z2 zoo, b2 museum. Each class at most 30 voters.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.hint.0: Choose and write one Class 1 vote set where zoo get 3 more than museum.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.hint.1: Choose Class 2 too, then compare combined zoo and museum votes.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.ok.c1: Vote counts natural numbers 0 or more.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Make vote numbers natural numbers 0 or more.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.ok.c2: For Class 1, zoo get 3 more votes.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.fail.c2: Class 1 zoo votes must be exactly 3 more than museum votes.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.ok.c3: For Class 2, museum get 2 more votes.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.fail.c3: Class 2 museum votes must be exactly 2 more than zoo votes.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.ok.c4: Each class get 30 voters or fewer.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.fail.c4: One class get over 30 voters. Reduce vote counts.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.ok.c5: When combine classes, zoo get 1 more vote.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.fail.c5: Combined difference no be 1. Check earlier conditions again.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.explain: Even with different vote counts, like 14·11·9·11, 5·2·3·5, 16·13·10·12, Class 1 zoo lead 3 and Class 2 museum lead 2; combined zoo always lead by 1. Counts differ but combined gap same.
z-m-07-08.s.s3.prompt: Friend say, 'We no know each class vote count, so can't know combined result.' How you answer? Use example numbers you make, separate wetin we know and no know.
z-m-07-08.s.s3.hint.0: You fit use numbers from your example as they be.
z-m-07-08.s.s3.hint.1: Separate friend's right point (we no know individual counts) from wrong point.
z-m-07-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You recalculate your example to check Class 1 and 2 differences really 3 and 2?
z-m-07-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You separate not knowing counts from knowing difference?
z-m-07-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You separately state wetin combined result can't tell, e.g. zoo vote total?
z-m-07-08.s.s3.model.0: We fit know without exact counts. Class 1 14 and 11, zoo lead 3; Class 2 9 and 11, museum lead 2. Combined zoo 23, museum 22, so zoo lead 1.
z-m-07-08.s.s3.modelNote.0: This answer no separately say vote totals for each place fit vary by example.
z-m-07-08.s.s3.model.1: No. We only need know how many more. Combine zoo lead 3 and museum lead 2, zoo lead 1. Same even if class voter counts differ.
z-m-07-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: Better also say we can't know exact zoo vote count.
z-m-07-08.s.s3.model.2: I no know vote count yet, but 3-2=1 show zoo lead 1. I can't say how many total zoo votes.

z-m-07-04.thinking.1: Change judgment and confidence with new information
z-m-07-04.title: Wetin colour be the 25th bead for the bead necklace?
z-m-07-04.topic: Match position (number) and colour for repeating arrangement
z-m-07-04.goal: Know the assumption wey you make wen you guess far-off value from rule wey you only see partly; talk how judgment and confidence change with new information, and find rule for numbers wey get the same colour.
z-m-07-04.material: Yoona dey make necklace, counting beads from front as 1st, 2nd, 3rd, ... The bead colours na red, blue and yellow, and e seem say rule dey for the colours wey she thread. I go tell you the colours with words only.
z-m-07-04.thinking.0: Guess rule from some data and test am
z-m-07-04.thinking.3: Make numbers wey fit the rule by yourself
z-m-07-04.prereq.0: Count things in line by numbering them 1st, 2nd, ...
z-m-07-04.prereq.1: Read arrangements where colours or shapes dey repeat (Grade 3 level)
z-m-07-04.s.s1.prompt: Make we guess as we learn the bead colours small small. Each step, choose wetin seem most likely.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.hint.0: Write the beads wey we know so far side by side, matching numbers and colours.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.hint.1: Find the first number where the same colour arrangement start again.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.info: The colours of beads 1 to 6 in order na red, blue, blue, yellow, red, blue.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Wetin colour you think 7th bead go be?
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.after: If you repeat red, blue, blue, yellow, the 7th go be blue. But we only see 6, so another rule still fit dey. So for now, both 'e seem blue' and 'e too early to decide' make sense.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Na guess say red, blue, blue, yellow dey repeat. We only pass one set small, so confidence no high.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You think say because yellow show for 4th, e go show for 7th too? Look the gap between number wey yellow show and number 7.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You think say because red show for 5th, red go continue? Look wetin colour be for 6th, directly after 5th.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: We no fit decide yet from only 6
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: E good to take care because only few beads show. But still look whether clue dey inside the beads wey you fit see.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Next, the colours of beads 7 to 12 in order na blue, yellow, red, blue, blue, yellow. Now we confirm all beads 1 to 12.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: If the rule continue, wetin colour you think 25th bead go be?
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.after: Up to 12, the same set of 4 repeat three times. Then 24th na last bead of sixth set (yellow), and 25th na first bead of new set, red. But 'rule continue' na assumption, so 'we no fit decide yet' na careful answer too.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: List the numbers wey yellow show: 4, 8, 12, then continue writing and check whether 25 dey among them.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: We only see 12, so we no fit decide yet
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: E good to be careful, but if you count how many times the same pattern repeat within 12, you fit find more clues.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Continue writing the numbers wey blue show: 2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 11, then check whether 25 dey among them.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Na judgment wey use sets wey repeat every 4 and point out where 25 dey for a new set.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Na new news. After necklace finish, we look 30th bead and e yellow. (We still no know beads 13 to 29.)
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Wetin happen to your thinking about 25th bead now?
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.after: If the rule hold, 30th suppose blue (30 na 2nd place after passing 7 sets of 4). But e yellow, so the rule fit change somewhere from 13 to 30. If the change happen after 25, 25th still red; if before, e fit change. So 'red, but less sure' and 'no fit decide' make sense, but 'sure' or 'yellow' no get support.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: 30th and 25th different numbers. Think whether 30th being yellow directly decide colour for 25th.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: No matter wetin 30th be, 25th surely red
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: First check whether 30th na the colour wey the rule predict. Work out what colour 30th suppose be if the rule hold.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: I still think say e red but I no sure as much as before
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Na judgment say even if new information shake the rule, if the place wey change dey after 25, 25th fit remain the same.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The rule fit don change somewhere, so we no fit decide the 25th
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Since we no know where rule change, na careful judgment. E depend whether the place wey change before or after 25.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.reflect: If you decide say 25th red, the news about 30th change the judgment itself or only reduce your confidence? Explain why how much you trust a rule wey you only see partly depend on how far you check.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.prompt: Seoyun assume say rule continue to 25th and find the 25th bead colour like this. Choose the line wey get mistake.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.hint.0: Try Seoyun method on 6th or 7th bead wey colour you already know, then compare with real colour.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.hint.1: Write the colours for beads numbered 1, 5, 9, 13 side by side and look wetin Seoyun method miss.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.line.0: The beads repeat red, blue, blue, yellow. One set get 4 beads.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.line.1: 25 divided by 4 give quotient 6 and remainder 1.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.line.2: Quotient na 6, so 25th bead get the same colour as 6th bead.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.line.3: 6th bead blue, so 25th bead blue too.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.explain: Line 3 wrong. Quotient only tell which set e dey, and remainder tell the position inside the set. If remainder na 1, e get same colour as 1st bead for the set (red). If you use the same method on 6th bead wey colour you know, quotient when you divide 6 by 4 na 1, so e match 1st bead (red), but real 6th bead na blue. The 'blue' for line 4 come from the mistake for line 3. If you do am correct, 25th na red.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.prompt: If the red, blue, blue, yellow rule continue, find and write 3 different bead numbers wey yellow. (Numbers from 1 to 40)
z-m-07-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write colours of beads 1 to 12 with their numbers and mark all numbers wey yellow.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.hint.1: Look at the gaps between marked numbers and continue with the same gap up to 40.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.fail.c1: Make the number a natural number from 1 to 40.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.fail.c2: Bead at this number no be yellow. Starting from the first number wey yellow show, count how many numbers apart yellow show.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.explain: Yellow na last bead of a set (4 beads), so e dey at numbers wey you count by 4, like 4, 8, 12, .... From 1 to 40, ten numbers dey: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.prompt: Write wetin common dey among the numbers you find, and talk why yellow show for those numbers.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.hint.0: Write the numbers you find in order from smallest and write the differences between them.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.hint.1: Remember which position inside a set yellow dey.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: You compare the numbers you write with table to check say dem all yellow?
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: You talk wetin common dey as the gap between numbers or the way of dividing?
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: You include for explanation which position inside a set yellow dey?
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.model.0: 4, 8 and 28 all be multiples of 4. One set get 4 beads and yellow na last one, so yellow show every 4 beads.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.model.1: If you divide the number by 4, remainder na 0. Yellow na fourth bead in a set, so e only dey at numbers wey remainder na 0.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.modelNote.1: Na answer wey put am as 'numbers wey divide exact'.

z-m-07-02.title: Can we find bigger number by comparing only digits after decimal point?
z-m-07-02.topic: Comparing one-decimal numbers (before and after decimal point)
z-m-07-02.goal: Know decimals compare from number before decimal point first; distinguish cases where comparing only decimal digits works and where it fails.
z-m-07-02.material: We measure three ribbons: 0.9m, 1.2m, 0.4m. Hyeonu wan order from shortest and think like this. (0.9 read 'zero point nine'; 1.2 'one point two.')
z-m-07-02.thinking.1: Making several numbers within a given range
z-m-07-02.prereq.0: Meaning, reading, writing one-decimal numbers (0.1, 1/10), number line (Grade 3)
z-m-07-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose wrong part in Hyeonu thinking.
z-m-07-02.s.s1.hint.0: First find which of 0.9m and 1.2m pass 1m.
z-m-07-02.s.s1.hint.1: Mark 0, 1, 2 on number line and place 0.4, 0.9, 1.2.
z-m-07-02.s.s1.line.1: We only compare digits after decimal: 9, 2, 4.
z-m-07-02.s.s1.explain: The mistake start at line 2: dem compare only digits after decimal. With decimal numbers, first compare whole-number part (1 and 0). 1.2 bigger than 1, while 0.9 less than 1, so 1.2 greater. Line 3 follow line 2 method and get wrong order (1.2m, 0.4m, 0.9m); line 4 conclude incorrectly '1.2m shortest.' Correct order na 0.4m, 0.9m, 1.2m. 2 is greater than 1.
z-m-07-02.s.s2.prompt: Write three different one-decimal numbers (units of 0.1) greater than 0.9 and less than 1.5.
z-m-07-02.s.s2.hint.0: Continue from 0.9, increasing by 0.1 each time.
z-m-07-02.s.s2.hint.1: Stop before 1.5 and check each number is in units of 0.1.
z-m-07-02.s.s2.ok.c1: E greater than 0.9 and less than 1.5.
z-m-07-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Must be greater than 0.9 and less than 1.5. Look between dem on number line.
z-m-07-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Write as units of 0.1 (one decimal place). Example 0.4, 1.2
z-m-07-02.s.s2.explain: One-decimal numbers between 0.9 and 1.5 na 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4: five. Add 0.1 to 0.9 give 1.0; stop before 1.5.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.prompt: When Hyeonu method 'compare only digits after decimal' work?
z-m-07-02.s.s3.hint.0: Make pairs like 0.4 and 0.9, 1.2 and 1.7, 0.9 and 1.2. Compare decimal-digit-only result with actual size; record right/wrong pairs.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.hint.1: Write what whole-number parts look like for correct pairs and incorrect pairs.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.o.a: Correct only when whole-number part na 0
z-m-07-02.s.s3.r.a: True for whole part 0, like 0.4 and 0.9. But check if works when whole parts same 1, like 1.2 and 1.7.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.o.b: Correct when numbers before decimal same
z-m-07-02.s.s3.r.b: If whole parts same, compare remaining part. If different, compare whole part first.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.o.c: Always correct when one digit follows decimal
z-m-07-02.s.s3.r.c: 1.2 and 0.9 also get one decimal digit, but method wrong. Decimal digit count alone no separate cases.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.r.d: 1.2 and 0.9 get different decimal digits but method wrong. Different digits not enough.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.explain: If numbers before decimal point same, comparing only after decimal point okay. For example, for 1.2 and 1.7, compare 2 and 7 show say 1.7 bigger. If numbers before decimal different, you must compare starting from the numbers before.

z-m-07-05.title: If we change the numbers for top row, the addition table pattern go change too?
z-m-07-05.topic: Pattern of how numbers change as you move across, down or diagonally in addition table
z-m-07-05.goal: Know say wen you move between boxes in addition table, how much number change depend on how much the row and column heading numbers change, and use this to design a table with the pattern you want.
z-m-07-05.material:
We make addition table. Numbers for left column na 1, 2, 3, 4 and numbers for top row na 2, 4, 6, 8. For box where row and column meet, write the total of the two numbers.

  + |  2   4   6   8
----+----------------
  1 |  3   5   7   9
  2 |  4   6   8  10
  3 |  5   7   9  11
  4 |  6   8  10  12

(Read with words: first row na 3, 5, 7, 9 / second row na 4, 6, 8, 10 / third row na 5, 7, 9, 11 / fourth row na 6, 8, 10, 12.) For textbook addition table, top row na 1, 2, 3, 4, so each step one box to the right make number bigger by 1.
z-m-07-05.thinking.0: Predict table pattern and check am
z-m-07-05.thinking.1: Find wrong reasoning when moving different directions
z-m-07-05.thinking.2: Design table wey meet the conditions by yourself
z-m-07-05.prereq.0: How to read addition table: write total of the two numbers in box where row and column meet (Grade 3 level)
z-m-07-05.prereq.1: Look at difference between numbers for neighboring boxes in table
z-m-07-05.s.s1.prompt: For this table, if you leave left column the same and change only top row to 3, 6, 9, 12, wetin happen to number wen you move one cell to the right for same row?
z-m-07-05.s.s1.hint.0: For table wey top row change to 3, 6, 9, 12, write the totals directly for row where left column na 1.
z-m-07-05.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether difference between two neighboring numbers same for other rows too (rows where left column na 2 or 3).
z-m-07-05.s.s1.r.a: Na correct for textbook table (top row 1, 2, 3, 4). But look how different two neighboring numbers for top row be.
z-m-07-05.s.s1.r.b: Na idea wey look how much top row change from 3 to 6 and 6 to 9, then notice say same change show for totals too.
z-m-07-05.s.s1.r.c: Increasing by 2 na change for original table (top row 2, 4, 6, 8). Look again how different neighboring numbers be for changed top row.
z-m-07-05.s.s1.o.d: E different for each box, so we no fit tell
z-m-07-05.s.s1.r.d: If you find difference between two neighboring boxes in same row for few places, you fit tell whether dem same or different.
z-m-07-05.s.s1.explain: For same row, number for left column stay same and only number for top row increase by 3, as in 3, 6, 9, 12. So wen you go one box to the right, total increase by 3 too. (If original table top row na 2, 4, 6, 8, e increase by 2.)
z-m-07-05.s.s2.prompt: Haeun explain how numbers change wen move between boxes in the table above like this. Choose line wey get mistake.
z-m-07-05.s.s2.hint.0: Find box wey get 7 in table and read number for box one step down-left.
z-m-07-05.s.s2.hint.1: Move down-left from other boxes too and write how much number change each time.
z-m-07-05.s.s2.line.0: Moving one box to the right make top-row number bigger by 2, so total bigger by 2.
z-m-07-05.s.s2.line.1: Moving one box down make left-column number bigger by 1, so total bigger by 1.
z-m-07-05.s.s2.line.2: So moving one box down-right make total bigger by 3.
z-m-07-05.s.s2.line.3: Then moving one box down-left make total smaller by 3.
z-m-07-05.s.s2.explain: Line 4 wrong. Moving one box down-left mean go one box left and reduce by 2, then go one box down and increase by 1. Reduce by 2 and increase by 1 make total smaller by 1. For example, move one box down-left from 7 in third box of first row; you reach 6 in second box of second row, wey smaller by 1. Lines 1 to 3 correct.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.prompt: Make our own addition table. Leave left column as 1, 2, 3, 4, and choose new numbers a, b, c for the first three boxes of top row so total go increase by 5 every time you move one box to right. Make 2 different tables. (From left, top row na a, b, c, and each na natural number from 1 to 30.)
z-m-07-05.s.s3.hint.0: Give one example how to choose top row so neighboring numbers differ by 5.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.hint.1: Using a,b,c you choose, write sums for first row (left column is 1) and check they grow by 5.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.fail.c1: Make a,b,c natural numbers from 1 to 30.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.ok.c2: From first box to second, increase by 5.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.fail.c2: a to b no increase by 5. Find difference.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.ok.c3: From second to third, increase by 5.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.fail.c3: b to c no increase by 5. Find difference.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.explain: If top row 1, 6, 11, sum increase by 5 each step right in same row. Other starts like 3,8,13 or 10,15,20 work too. Key na adjacent top numbers differ by 5. 1, 6, 11; 3, 8, 13; 10, 15, 20.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.because.prompt: Explain how you choose top row and why sum grow by 5 as you move right.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.because.hint.0: Write sums of left-column 1 plus first and second top-row numbers, then find difference.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.because.hint.1: When sum change, point to which of the two numbers change.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: You write sums for first row using your numbers and check growth really 5?
z-m-07-05.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: You explain left-column number stay same while only top-row numbers change?
z-m-07-05.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: You fit say how both tables same and different?
z-m-07-05.s.s3.because.model.0: I make top row increase by 5, like 1,6,11. In same row left-column number stay same, top-row number increase 5, so sum increase 5 too. 1, 6, 11.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.because.model.1: I choose 3,8,13. If one added number (left column) stay same and other (top) increase 5, sum increase 5 too. 3, 8, 13.
z-m-07-05.s.s3.because.modelNote.1: This answer explain same reason using words 'numbers added.'
z-m-07-05.s.s3.because.model.2: I use 1,6,11. Left number same, top number only one grow by 5, so sum grow 5 too. 1, 6, 11.

z-m-07-06.title: If you stick two identical right triangles, you always get rectangle?
z-m-07-06.topic: Shapes from sticking two same right triangles (shape and perimeter)
z-m-07-06.goal: Test claim 'always' by changing sides and joining methods to find counterexample; explain how perimeter change when joined edge hidden.
z-m-07-06.material:
Two colored-paper right triangles have exactly same size/shape. Sides next to right angle 3 cm and 4 cm; longest side 5 cm. Join equal-length sides exactly, no gap or overlap, to make new shape. You fit flip or turn paper before joining.
Seoa say, 'Two identical right triangles always make rectangle!'
(3 cm read 'three centimeters.')
z-m-07-06.thinking.0: Separate when claim true and false
z-m-07-06.thinking.1: Find counterexamples by changing joined side
z-m-07-06.thinking.2: Explain how joined side affect perimeter
z-m-07-06.prereq.1: Perimeter na distance all the way around shape edge
z-m-07-06.s.s1.prompt: Wetin you think about Seoa statement?
z-m-07-06.s.s1.hint.0: Use paper make two right triangles (3cm,4cm,5cm) and draw shapes as you change joined side. If no paper, imagine right angle like book corner and do mentally.
z-m-07-06.s.s1.hint.1: For joined shape, check whether all four angles right and whether four sides dey.
z-m-07-06.s.s1.o.a: E depend how you join dem
z-m-07-06.s.s1.r.a: You plan check by changing joined side and direction. Find cases where result rectangle to make am clear.
z-m-07-06.s.s1.o.b: You no fit know before you join
z-m-07-06.s.s1.r.b: You know right angles and side lengths, so you fit work am out mentally. Remember whether rectangle get four right angles.
z-m-07-06.s.s1.o.c: Any way you join, e never become rectangle
z-m-07-06.s.s1.r.c: You check whether no joining method make rectangle? Look again at longest-side case.
z-m-07-06.s.s1.o.d: Any way you join, e become rectangle
z-m-07-06.s.s1.r.d: You follow Seoa claim directly. Also make/check 3 cm side case yourself.
z-m-07-06.s.s1.explain: If join 5cm sides and turn one piece, rectangle 3cm wide and 4cm high. If join 3cm sides, flipping make large triangle; turning make slanted quadrilateral, no rectangle. So depend on joined side and orientation.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.prompt: Find perimeter of joined shape. One triangle perimeter 12cm. If equal sides length j cm (one of 3,4,5) join, find two different cases where new shape perimeter pass 14cm. 3 cm and 4 cm.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.hint.0: First find total perimeters of both pieces.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.hint.1: Use paper check whether joined side stay on outside edge; subtract length wey no remain visible.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.ok.c1: Na side wey fit be joined.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Joined side must be 3, 4, or 5 cm. Pieces identical, so join same-length sides.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.fail.c2: Perimeter no pass 14cm. Check if some side hide inside joint.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.explain: One piece perimeter 3+4+5=12cm; two total 24cm. Joined side hide inside on both pieces. Join 3cm sides: 24−6=18cm; 4cm: 24−8=16cm; 5cm: 24−10=14cm. Perimeter >14 when joining 3 or 4cm side.
z-m-07-06.s.s3.prompt: Wetin you wan tell Seoa? Give one joining method that make rectangle and one that no; say which side and how.
z-m-07-06.s.s3.hint.0: Remember cases joining 3cm, 4cm, 5cm sides from perimeter task, one by one.
z-m-07-06.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many right angles shape get after joining.
z-m-07-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: With joining method you describe, did you check four angles to confirm rectangle or no?
z-m-07-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You clearly state joined side by its length?
z-m-07-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You know one counterexample enough to break 'always'?
z-m-07-06.s.s3.model.0: E no always so. If join 5cm sides and turn one, rectangle 3cm by 4cm; but if join 3cm sides, no rectangle.
z-m-07-06.s.s3.model.1: Depend on joined side. Join longest sides and rectangle fit form, but join short 4cm sides and no rectangle.
z-m-07-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: Writing only 'short side' okay, but length make am clearer.

z-m-07-10.title: Wetin results Seoha and Haram draw tell about two bags?
z-m-07-10.topic: Results fit differ even under same conditions (possibility)
z-m-07-10.goal: Learn not conclude bags differ from few results in 10 draws; say how far results be clues and how to check more.
z-m-07-10.material:
Two bags mix red and blue marbles (가, 나). We don't know marbles per bag or whether bags same. Seoha draw from 가 and Haram from 나, check color and replace each time, 10 draws each.
Bag 가 (Seoha): red 7, blue 3
Bag 나 (Haram): red 4, blue 6
Seoha say, 'My bag get more red and Haram bag more blue. Bags different!'
z-m-07-10.thinking.0: Checking whether results alone allow conclusion
z-m-07-10.prereq.0: Counting outcomes by frequency and organizing in table
z-m-07-10.s.s1.prompt: Wetin you think about Seoha? Choose best response based only on result.
z-m-07-10.s.s1.hint.0: Put Seoha and Haram results side by side in table.
z-m-07-10.s.s1.hint.1: Suppose both draw same bag; could these results happen?
z-m-07-10.s.s1.o.a: We can't say anything from results
z-m-07-10.s.s1.r.a: Results still clue. Bag with more red draws may be somewhat more likely to have more red. Jumping to conclusion and ignoring clue are different.
z-m-07-10.s.s1.o.b: Bag 가 has more red and 나 more blue
z-m-07-10.s.s1.r.b: You accept Seoha words directly. Could 10 draws from same bag vary this much?
z-m-07-10.s.s1.o.c: Bag 가 has 7 red marbles and 나 has 4
z-m-07-10.s.s1.r.c: Draw count no equal marble count. Since replace each time, same marble could come many times.
z-m-07-10.s.s1.o.d: From only 10 draws, can't conclude bags different
z-m-07-10.s.s1.r.d: This accepts results as clue but sees more checking needed. Remember same bag can give different results.
z-m-07-10.s.s1.explain: Even from same bag, 10 draws each fit give red 7 or 4. Different results no prove bags different, but result still clue: side with more red draws may have slightly higher chance of more red marbles.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.prompt: Which methods help find out better whether bags same/different? Choose all helpful.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.hint.0: For each method, write new information you'd get.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.hint.1: Compare trusting first results with collecting new ones.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.o.a: Each method increase draw count and combine results
z-m-07-10.s.s2.r.a: As draw count grow, result tend to approach bag's marble ratio, making clue more trustworthy.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.o.b: Trust which side got more red in current draws
z-m-07-10.s.s2.r.b: Trusting current results adds no information, so first judgment no stronger.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.o.c: Each draw one more and decide by that color
z-m-07-10.s.s2.r.c: One extra draw tells very little. Need many draws to build clue.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.o.d: Take all marbles out and count colors
z-m-07-10.s.s2.r.d: Direct count gives strongest certainty if allowed. If game no allow removing, cannot use.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.explain: More draws combined strengthen clue; taking out and counting confirms directly. Trusting current result or drawing just once more gives little new info.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.acc.0: If game no let you remove/count, increasing and combining draws best method.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.acc.1: If you can take them out and count, you know for sure. Also consider more draws if you can't.
z-m-07-10.s.s3.prompt: Wetin you wan tell Seoha? Say how to check further while respecting her result.
z-m-07-10.s.s3.hint.0: Start with fact Seoha and Haram each draw 10 times.
z-m-07-10.s.s3.hint.1: Separate part of Seoha result you can trust from part not certain.
